However, she notes a structural gap: fund managers currently accept on-chain subscriptions but must invest the underlying portfolio into off-chain instruments during normal business hours, limiting yield generation overnight. Full efficiency requires the underlying liquid instruments (Treasuries, bonds) to also be tokenized and accessible on-chain. Digital custody, wallet/key management, and traditional asset servicing also need to be in place. Legal recognition, settlement finality, AML and KYC frameworks must accompany the technology for the system to scale safely.
quote: A tokenized money market fund at the end of the day is a portfolio of different liquid instruments like US Treasuries, bonds and other things like that. It's a common standard widely adopted, basically in our conversation with end, when we spend very little time to really agree on the message standard, because that message standard widely accepted can be easily understood by both teams, right. headline: China's structural savings surplus is the primary driver of global imbalances, with US deficits a consequence rather than a cause; adjustment in China would reduce imbalances worldwide
reasoning: Pettis presents three competing theories of global imbalances and rejects the view that US under-saving drives Chinese over-saving. He argues it is more plausible that a country controlling its external account (China) exports domestic imbalances to countries that do not (the US). His forthcoming book addresses this directly. The implication is that rebalancing China's economy would also rebalance other major economies as a by-product, not the reverse.
quote: I would argue that if you look at the Chinese economy, it's very hard to argue that the imbalances in the Chinese economy, which are the most extreme in history, are a result of China's need to accommodate Los Aided in the U.S. I would turn it around. And I would also argue that it's more likely for a country that controls its external account to export domestic imbalances than it is for a country that doesn't control its external account. So what I would argue is that as the Chinese imbalances of just, much of the remaining imbalances in the world would also adjust.

headline: Fiscal expansion not a viable rebalancing tool given China's total debt-to-GDP already at 320% and rising faster than any other country in history; adjustment likely to mean significant growth slowdown or decades of stagnation

He contrasts this with US concerns about 10 percentage points over 5–10 years. While raising the household income share of GDP is widely recognised as the necessary fix, transferring income from government or business is politically and economically disruptive, and further expanding fiscal deficits risks breaching debt capacity. Historical analogies — the US contraction of the 1930s and Japan's post-1991 stagnation — suggest the adjustment will not be painless.

Well, as you know, in China, we do more than that every year... any country that has had very, very low consumption and very rapid growth in debt along with a large trade surplus, we've seen this many times before, never as extreme as China's, but we've seen this many times before, they always adjust either in the form of an economic contraction, like the U.S. hit in the 1930s, or in the form of decades of stagnation, like Chip had did after 1991. So I'm not sure there's a way to do this that doesn't involve a significant slowdown in growth.
